section: PART 2 - Specify Competing & Estimate Regression Models
text:
PART 2 - Specify Competing & Estimate Regression Models

Predicting Patterns
In this dataset, we have the outcome variable, being those that survived, based on the predict values being age, socioeconomic status (SES) and sex. Based on on the social and political climate of 1912, the survival of individuals would likely reflect specific factors. For example, those with a first class ticket are likely of a higher SES, and within this time period may have been viewed as more “valuable”, prioritizing their lives over the lives of those in third class. Additionally, based on the lower quantities of women and a lower valuation of worth within this time in history, it may be thought that there may be a significantly lower proportion of women that survived, compared to men, even when considering the initial proportions. Finally, I expect that the survivors will likely be of lower age, potentially below 30. This would be for reasons pertaining to ocean survival in the lifeboats, and a longer lifespan ahead of them after being rescued, as unfortunate as these ideas are.


Specifying Four Nested Models


Code
#2.2 - Specifying Nested Models 

#Intercept-Only model 
model0 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ 1,data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

#Survival Based on Sex  
model1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex, 
  data = titanic, 
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

#Survival Based on Sex + Ticket Class 
model2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass, 
  data = titanic, 
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

#Survival Based on Sex + Ticket Class + Age 
model3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age, 
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))


Pay particular attention to: The interpretation of the intercept changes between model1, model2, and model3. We can see that as the predictors are being added, there is an increase in the estimated intercept, being code, code, code, respectively. The first intercept in model1 is a reflection of the females on board, as seen by the “Sexmale” category being code, showing the coefficient of their lesser likelihood of surviving compared to women. In model2, however when adding the Pclass, the intercept increased to code, being the log-odds of survival of the females in first class, as seen by the Sexmale decreasing to code, showing the males in first class have similar likelihood of survival as females (as we’ve held class constant with little coefficient change), followed by the Pclass 2 and 3 which have increasingly worse survival rates. Finally, in model3 with the addition of age, whose slope coefficient is code, meaning that every year added decreases the log-oddsd of survival by such value. This means that those who were younger had a higher survival weight. The slope coefficients showing a decreased rate of survival is due to their negative value, showing that the inclusion of that specific predictor value would decrease the odds of survival, as seen throughout their addition in each model. Looking at the AIC and BIC which penalize complexity (added predictors) when not increasing the predictive value of the equations. However, it can be seen that there is a desirable decrease in both AIC and BIC throughout the models, with model3 exhibiting the smallest of both and how this model is optimal.

tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)



Evaluating Predictors & Model Fit

As Sex was added from the intercept only model, sex can explain significantly more variation, as explained in a few of the produced values. The change in Degrees of Freedom shows the extra row of male versus female, the X2 statistic, whose value exhibits the decrease in deviance, so the larger the number, the better the fit of the model. We can see that there was a large increase, χ²(1) = 213.82, p < .001 in this value, meaning that the model has a better fit and accounts for significantly more variation than the intercept model alone. Additionally, the Pr(>Chisq) value shows high levels of significance.
The Pclass additionally improves model fit beyond sex, as seen by another substantially large value, χ²(2) = 78.27, p < .001 degrees of freedom, in the Chisq column (χ² statistic), representing a drop in deviance, reflecting a better-fitting model. Although it is not as large as the change from model0 to model1, the number is adequate to believe that it positively impacts the predictive value of the model. There was no change in the p-value, however.
Finally, adding age does improve the model fit beyond the value of ‘Sex’ and ‘Pclass’, however according ot the χ² value, the least out of all predictors, as it was only as it was only χ²(1) = 25.15, p < .001. However, this change is enough to believe that the addition of ‘Age’ does have a positive effect on model fit. There was an small increase in the p-value, but it is still showing significance and is not reflective on the value of the predictor. It should be noted that the change in the degrees of freedom is reflective of the addition of new predictors/rows within the model.



Extract Overall Model Performance


Code
#3.2 - Extracting Metrics into "Glance"
glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(model0)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(model1)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(model2)
glance3 <- broom.mixed::glance(model3)

#Renaming the Models
models <- c(
  "model0: Null",
  "model1: Sex",
  "model2: + Pclass",
  "model3: + Age")

#Combining the rows 
glances <- rbind(glance0, glance1, glance2, glance3)




Code
#3.3 - Combining sets of results 
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = models,
  glances,
  tests)

Interpreting Comparisons
When examining the outputted table, the model fit and complexity is reflected through the AIC and BIC values, with lower values indicating a balance between complexity and fit, and an even stronger penalty for complexity (respectively). With these criteria, the models with the lowest AIC and BIC values, being model 3, with (AIC = comparison_table$AIC[4], BIC = comparison_table$BIC[4]), it would be the best fit to the data. As the predictors are added, the AIC and BIC values decrease significantly between all models as predictors are added, however the smallest decrease in BIC values was found between models 2 and 3 through the addition of the ‘Age’ predictor, yet this was the smallest improvement. While examining the likelihood-ratio tests (LRT), a larger number that the previous model is desirable, as it means that the deviance has decreased through this more complex model. When additional predictors are added, the LRT scores increase noticeably, as they become less and less negative. Similar to the AIC and BIC tests, however, although the scores still exhibit an increase in the LRT value, there is a significantly smaller increase in values from model 2 to model 3 (similar to the pattern of decreases seen in the AIC and BIC scores). The largest differences in AIC, BIC and LRT scores are seen from model 0 to model 1 (naturally), then from model 1 to model 2, and the smallest differences from model 2 to model 3 - again, these are consistent across metrics. This would reflect that the ‘Sex’ and ‘PClass’ predictors accounting for a greater variance than ‘Age’, providing a greater contribution. All of the above do have a nested p value of <0.001, once more highlighting the improvement of model fit.

title: Binary Logistic Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
In this lab, you will apply binary logistic regression analysis to investigate the factors associated with surviving the Titanic crash. Rather than estimating a single binary logistic regression model, you will develop and compare a series of competing models, evaluate their performance, examine binary logistic regression diagnostics, and interpret the results of your preferred model.
Your goal is to produce a reproducible statistical report that demonstrates not only how to estimate binary logistic regression models, but also how to make and justify decisions about model specification and selection.
You will complete the analysis in R, document your workflow in Quarto, and publish the rendered report using GitHub Pages.


By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Specify multiple binary logistic regression models based on substantive predictions.
Estimate and compare nested binary logistic regression models using AIC, BIC and likelihood-ratio tests.
Evaluate binary logistic regression assumptions and identify potentially influential observations.
Select a preferred model and justify that decision.
Extract, report, and interpret binary logistic regression coefficients using broom.mixed::tidy().
Visualize your data using the ggeffects::gpredict()
Communicate your analysis in a reproducible Quarto report.

Part 1: Configure your project and examine the data

1.1. Create your project
Create a new GitHub repository for this lab, following the workflow established in Lab 1.
Your repository should contain:

An RStudio project connected to your GitHub repository.
An index.qmd file containing your analysis and written report.
A _quarto.yml file configured to render your report to the docs/ directory.
A docs/ directory containing the rendered website.

Your analysis must be reproducible from the files in your repository.
Important: As in Lab 1, you should distinguish between commands used for interactive exploration in the R Console and commands required to reproduce your results in Quarto.
You may use the Console to inspect datasets, experiment with model specifications, and troubleshoot errors. However, every command necessary to generate the results presented in your report must appear in your Quarto document.


1.2. Load the required packages
You will need the following packages:

dplyr and tidyr for data manipulation.
ggplot2 for visualization.
broom.mixed for extracting binary logistic regression results.
performance for binary logistic regression diagnostics and model comparisons.
gt for formatting tables.
ggeffects for binary logistic regression visualization

Install any missing packages in the R Console. Load the packages in a setup chunk near the beginning of your Quarto document.

Part 3: Compare model performance
You will compare the four models using nested-model χ²-tests and two measures of overall performance.

3.1. Conduct nested-model χ²-tests
Use anova() to compare all four models in a single call, in the order mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3.
The resulting table will allow you to evaluate three questions:

Does Sex explain significantly more variation than the intercept-only model?
Does adding Pclass improve model fit beyond Sex?
Does adding Age increase improve model fit beyond Sex and Pclass?

Residual degrees of freedom.
Change in degrees of freedom.

p-value for the nested-model comparison.

3.2. Extract nested model-level performance statistics
Use broom.mixed::glance() to extract nested model-level statistics for each of the four fitted models.

Include a column identifying each model.
For this lab, focus on:

BIC: Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity. Lower values are preferred.
Likelihood-ratio test (χ²): Tests whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit relative to the preceding model. A statistically significant p-value (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictors improve model fit.

Part 4: Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

4.1. Examine the assumptions
Select the most promising model based on your comparisons in Part 3.
Evaluate the following binary logistic regression assumptions:

Linearity to the logit scale: Is the relationship between predictors and the outcome adequately represented by the model? Is the residual variability reasonably uniform across fitted values? (use DHARMa:: diagnostic plots)
Collinearity: Are predictors so strongly related that their unique contributions may be difficult to estimate precisely?
Complete separation: Does any predictor perfectly predict the outcome variable?
Influential observations: Are there observations that may disproportionately influence the fitted model? (use DHARMa:: again)
Events per predictor: Are there enough events for each coefficient of your predictor variable? 



4.2. Report your diagnostic findings
Include at least one set of diagnostic plots in your Quarto report.
Write a short paragraph explaining:

Which assumptions appear reasonably satisfied.
Whether any potential problems are evident.
Whether those problems affect your confidence in or interpretation of the model.

Avoid treating binary logistic regression assumptions as a mechanical checklist. Explain what the diagnostic results imply for the interpretation of your findings.

4. Nested Model Comparisons
We will evaluate the models. Our main performance metrics are:

AIC: Evaluates model fit while penalizing model complexity. Lower values indicate a preferred balance between fit and complexity.
BIC: Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity. Lower values are preferred.
Likelihood-ratio test (χ²): Tests whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit relative to the preceding model. A statistically significant p-value (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictors improve model fit.


4.1. Compare the models

4.5. Interpreting the combined table
Each row represents one fitted binary logistic regression model.
When comparing models, we generally look for lower AIC and BIC values and whether the likelihood-ratio test indicates a statistically significant improvement in model fit.
For example, the mod2 row tells us how well mod2 fits the data relative to mod1, considering both model fit and complexity (AIC, BIC). The likelihood-ratio test is significant, telling us that adding avoidance as a predictor significantly improves model fit beyond satisfaction.
The mod3 comparison tests whether adding cohabitation significantly improves model fit after accounting for satisfaction and avoidance. For mod3, the likelihood-ratio test is significant, AIC is lower, however, BIC slightly increases. Given how minimally BIC increases, mod3 is our preferred model.
Remember: The mod0 row has no incremental comparison because it serves as the baseline.


Additional performance comparison

For this demonstration, we will use the likelihood-ratio test as an initial selection criterion. We can see that the likelihood ratio test is still significant for our most complex model, mod3. 8. Interpret the results

8.1. Coefficients are on the log-odds scale


Code
fixef(mod3)



Conditional model:
  (Intercept)   satisfaction      avoidance  cohabitingYes  
      -2.7690         0.8019        -0.4001         0.5916  


The coefficients represent changes in the log-odds of staying together at 12 months, holding the other predictors constant.
For a one-point increase in satisfaction, holding avoidance and cohabiting status constant, the log-odds of staying together increase by 0.8.
For a one-point increase in avoidance, holding satisfaction and cohabiting status constant, the log-odds of staying together decrease by 0.4.
The coefficient for cohabitingYes represents the log-odds difference between cohabiting and non-cohabiting couples, holding satisfaction and avoidance constant. Recall that not cohabiting is our reference group, therefore the log-odds of staying together increase by 0.59 when couples live together compared to when they do not , holding satisfaction and avoidance constant.


8.2 Transform log-odds into odds ratios
Exponentiating the coefficients transforms them from log-odds into odds ratios.

We fit a binomial GLM with a logit link predicting 12-month relationship status from satisfaction, attachment avoidance, and cohabiting status. Higher satisfaction was associated with higher odds of remaining together, OR = 2.23, 95% CI [1.75, 2.83]. Higher attachment avoidance was associated with lower odds of remaining together, OR = 0.67, 95% CI [0.53, 0.85]. Cohabiting couples had higher odds of remaining together compared to non-cohabiting couples, OR = 1.81, 95% CI [1.1, 2.96].

This analysis illustrates how relationship dissolution can be investigated using several competing binary logistic regression models.
The model-comparison process allows us to evaluate whether additional predictors explain meaningful variation beyond simpler models.
The final model provides estimates of the odds of a couple staying together or dissolving.

text:
2 - Specify Competing & Estimate Regression Models

Predicting Patterns
In this dataset, we have the outcome variable, being those that survived, based on the predict values being age, socioeconomic status (SES) and sex. Based on on the social and political climate of 1912, the survival of individuals would likely reflect specific factors. For example, those with a first class ticket are likely of a higher SES, and within this time period may have been viewed as more “valuable”, prioritizing their lives over the lives of those in third class. Additionally, based on the lower quantities of women and a lower valuation of worth within this time in history, it may be thought that there may be a significantly lower proportion of women that survived, compared to men, even when considering the initial proportions. Finally, I expect that the survivors will likely be of lower age, potentially below 30. This would be for reasons pertaining to ocean survival in the lifeboats, and a longer lifespan ahead of them after being rescued, as unfortunate as these ideas are.


Specifying Four Nested Models


Code
#2.2 - Specifying Nested Models 

#Intercept-Only model 
model0 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ 1,data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

#Survival Based on Sex  
model1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex, 
  data = titanic, 
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

#Survival Based on Sex + Ticket Class 
model2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass, 
  data = titanic, 
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

#Survival Based on Sex + Ticket Class + Age 
model3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age, 
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))


Pay particular attention to: The interpretation of the intercept changes between model1, model2, and model3. We can see that as the predictors are being added, there is an increase in the estimated intercept, being 1.12, 2.33, and 3.78, respectively. The first intercept in model1 is a reflection of the females on board, as seen by the “Sexmale” category being (-2.48), showing the coefficient of their lesser likelihood of surviving compared to women. In model2, however when adding the Pclass, the intercept increased to 2.33, being the log-odds of survival of the females in first class, as seen by the Sexmale decreasing to -2.57, showing the males in first class have similar likelihood of survival as females (as we’ve held class constant with little coefficient change), followed by the Pclass 2 (-0.93) and 3 (-1.97) which have increasingly worse survival rates. Finally, in model3 with the addition of age, whose slope coefficient is 3.78, meaning that every year added decreases the log-odds of survival by such value. This means that those who were younger had a higher odds of survival. The slope coefficients showing a decreased rate of survival is due to their negative value, showing that the inclusion of that specific predictor value would decrease the odds of survival, as seen throughout their addition in each model. Looking at the AIC and BIC which penalize complexity (added predictors) when not increasing the predictive value of the equations. However, it can be seen that there is a desirable decrease in both AIC and BIC throughout the models, with model3 exhibiting the smallest of both and how this model best-fitting

We took data from the titanic and used four nested binary logistic regression models using predictors of Sex, Age, and Socioeconomic Class (Pclass). The models began with the intercept model (Model0) being just the survival, Model1 being Sex, Model 2 being added Pclass and Model 3 being the added Age variable. The results that were found were decreasing AIC & BIC as the models increased complexity with the addition of predictors, reflecting Model 3 accounting for the most variability and best predictive abilities. Model 3 additionally had larger LRT scores, thus being selected as the ideal models with an AIC of (657.28) and BIC of (680.14).
The results of the preferred model are as follows. With females being the reference group, the males had 0.08 times the log odds of survival compared to females, with a 95% CI being [r round(or_ci[“Sexmale”, 1], 2), r round(or_ci[“Sexmale”, 2], 2)]. When examining the outputted table, the model fit and complexity is reflected through the AIC and BIC values, with lower values indicating a balance between complexity and fit, and an even stronger penalty for complexity (respectively). When additional predictors are added, the LRT scores increase noticeably, as they become less and less negative. Similar to the AIC and BIC tests, however, although the scores still exhibit an increase in the LRT value, there is a significantly smaller increase in values from model 2 to model 3 (similar to the pattern of decreases seen in the AIC and BIC scores). The largest differences in AIC, BIC and LRT scores are seen from model 0 to model 1 (naturally), then from model 1 to model 2, and the smallest differences from model 2 to model 3 - again, these are consistent across metrics. This would reflect that the ‘Sex’ and ‘PClass’ predictors accounting for a greater variance than ‘Age’, providing a greater contribution. All of the above do have a nested p value of <0.001, once more highlighting the improvement of model fit.

Results Paragraph
In this statistical analysis, we used a binary GLM and the use of the logit link in order to assess the factors of Sex, Age, and Socioeconomic status (Pclass/SES). As a whole, females compared to males had higher odds of survival, 0.08, 95% CI [0.05, 0.12], 0.12]. This means that women were prioritized for their survival over men. When accounting for the SES, a higher class (first class over second or third) was associated with higher odds of surviving in both women and men. Decreased odds of survival seen in second class 0.27, 95% CI [0.16, 0.47], versus decreased odds of survival in third class 0.08, 95% CI [0.04, 0.13]. As a whole, those with a higher social status and “financial standing” were given a greater chance of survival. Finally, when accounting for age, it was seen that every additional year of age was associated in a decrease in odds of survival, 0.96, 95% CI [0.95, 0.98]. This shows that the priority was given to those who were younger, and even kids - similar to the prediction of the model. As seen in the movies, women, children and the rich were given priority over the alternate.
